Common questions

How much storage does a vector index actually use?

Raw bytes are vectorCount × dimension × 4 (float32) plus any metadata stored per vector. A million 1536-dimension embeddings (OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small size) is about 5.7 GiB of raw vectors before any index structure is built. The index itself — an HNSW graph, quantization bookkeeping, replication — adds overhead on top of that, and how much varies by engine and tuning, so this calculator asks for an overhead multiplier you set rather than assuming one for you.

Why doesn't this calculator show live Pinecone, Weaviate, or Qdrant prices?

Because a wrong number is worse than no number, and vendor pricing changes. This calculator does the arithmetic — storage sizing and the cost formula — from rates you paste in from each provider's own current pricing page. It never fetches or asserts a vendor's price on its own.

What is a reasonable index overhead multiplier to use?

There is no single correct number — it depends on the index type and its build parameters. Start at 1.0 to see the raw vector size alone, then check your chosen provider's own documentation or measure your actual deployed index size and set the multiplier so the calculator's storage estimate matches what you observed. See what is index overhead for the longer version.

Does this calculator upload my numbers anywhere?

No. Every field runs in your browser; nothing is sent to a server. An optional anonymous local counter records which buttons get used, never the numbers you typed, and can be turned off.

vs-doing-the-math-yourself.html.text:
← Vector Database Cost Calculator

This calculator vs. doing the math yourself

Reading each provider's pricing page for its current rates is still on you either way -- this tool never fetches or asserts a vendor's price. What it takes off your plate is sizing the index correctly and running the free-tier-and-rate arithmetic across every provider without a slip.

What each approach actually involves

Doing it yourself means opening each provider's pricing page, noting its storage rate, its query rate, and any free allowance, then estimating how big your index actually is. The estimate most people reach for by hand is vectorCount × dimension × 4 bytes, converted to gigabytes -- the raw embedding size. Then, for every provider: subtract its free storage and query allowance from your totals, multiply each remainder by that provider's rate, add storage cost to query cost, and repeat for the next provider.

This calculator takes the same rates a pricing-page lookup gives you and the same vector count, dimension, and metadata size you would estimate from by hand -- plus an index-overhead multiplier you set yourself, the piece a raw-bytes shortcut leaves out -- and runs the storage sizing and the per-provider free-tier-and-rate arithmetic for up to three providers at once, ranked cheapest first.

Worked exampleDoing it yourself (raw vectors only)This calculator
1,000,000 vectors × 1536 dimensions, 200 B metadata/vector, 1.3× index overhead5.72 GB — vectorCount × dimension × 4, metadata and overhead left out7.68 GB — raw vectors + metadata, ×1.3 overhead
Provider A: $0.33/GB storage, $8/million queries, no free tier — at 5 million queries/month$41.89/month total$42.53/month total
Provider B: $0.25/GB storage, $5/million queries, 1 GB + 1 million queries free — at 5 million queries/month$21.18/month total$21.67/month total

The two totals are the calculator's own default inputs, so you can load them on the calculator page and check the arithmetic yourself. The raw-vectors-only shortcut understates this index's storage by about 26% (5.72 GB against the real 7.68 GB) because it counts float32 embeddings only and leaves out both the metadata payload and the index structure a deployed database actually builds on top of them -- the exact gap this calculator's own index overhead field exists to let you account for instead of guessing away. Query cost happens to dominate both totals here, so the ranking does not flip in this example -- but the dollar gap between the two storage estimates scales with index size, and on a storage-heavy workload with a provider's free tier sized close to your real footprint, an understated estimate is exactly the kind of error that puts you on the wrong side of a free-tier boundary without knowing it.

Common questions

Why not just read each provider's pricing page and do the arithmetic myself?

You still have to -- this calculator does not fetch or assert any vendor's price, so the rates always come from you reading the vendor's own current pricing page. What doing it by hand also requires is sizing your index in gigabytes first, then for every provider you are comparing: subtracting its free storage and query allowance, multiplying the remainder by its rate, and adding storage cost to query cost. That is a few minutes of careful arithmetic per provider, repeated for each one, with no check on whether a subtraction or a decimal point slipped.

What does a hand-rolled storage estimate usually get wrong?

The shortcut most people reach for is vectorCount times dimension times 4 bytes, then convert to gigabytes and stop there. That is the raw embedding size only. A deployed index adds structure on top of it -- an HNSW graph, quantization bookkeeping, replication -- plus whatever metadata payload rides along with each vector, and both are easy to leave out of a back-of-envelope number because they are not part of the obvious formula. See the worked example above for how much that omission understates the real footprint.

Is comparing three providers by hand really that error-prone?

Each provider adds its own free-storage allowance, free-query allowance, storage rate, and query rate -- four numbers to keep straight, repeated for every provider in the comparison, with a subtraction and two multiplications each. Getting one provider's arithmetic right by hand is easy. Keeping all of them consistent across three providers, and re-doing all of it the next time a rate or your workload changes, is where a hand count and a mechanical one start to diverge.

Does this calculator upload anything I enter?

No. Every field runs in your browser, the same as doing the arithmetic on paper -- there is no account, no server call, and no analytics vendor. The only difference is the calculator does not mis-add the columns.

← Vector Database Cost Calculator

This calculator vs. Pinecone's own pricing page

Two different jobs: Pinecone's pricing page documents Pinecone's own plans and how Pinecone bills for its own service. This page estimates the storage footprint of one workload and prices it identically across Pinecone and other vector database providers, side by side, using the rates you paste in.

What each tool is for

Pinecone's pricing page is Pinecone's own documentation of its plans, usage-based unit pricing, and how those units are billed for Pinecone specifically. It answers "what would this workload cost on Pinecone" for Pinecone alone, using Pinecone's own current numbers. Pinecone's own site is not reachable from this session to confirm today's specific plan names, unit prices, or free-tier limits, so no dollar figure for Pinecone appears anywhere on this page — only its well-documented identity and category are stated here.

This calculator does a different, narrower job: it does not describe any single vendor's plan structure. You type in your vector count, embedding dimension, and any per-vector metadata size once; it computes the resulting storage footprint in gigabytes, including an index-overhead multiplier you set yourself rather than one this tool assumes on your behalf. You then paste in the storage and query rates quoted by up to three providers — Pinecone included, if you want it in the comparison — and it totals a monthly estimate for each, ranked cheapest first. It runs free in any browser, keeps no account, and nothing you type is uploaded.

what-is-vector-index-overhead.html.text:
← Vector Database Cost Calculator

What is vector index overhead?

Raw vector bytes are one number: vector count × dimension × 4 bytes for float32, plus any metadata you store alongside each vector. What a deployed, queryable index actually occupies is usually more — here is why, and how to pick a number instead of guessing.

Why a deployed index is bigger than the raw vectors

A vector database does not just store your embeddings — it builds a data structure on top of them so that a similarity search does not have to compare your query against every stored vector one by one. That structure costs space. Three common contributors, though the exact mix and magnitude is engine- and configuration-specific:

  • Graph or tree structure. HNSW (Hierarchical Navigable Small World) is the most common approach in production vector databases today: it stores links between nearby vectors across multiple layers so a search can skip most of the dataset instead of scanning it. Those links are extra data on top of the vectors themselves, and denser graphs (more links per node, more layers) trade more storage for faster or more accurate search.
  • Quantization bookkeeping. Some engines compress vectors for storage and search (product quantization, scalar quantization, binary quantization) to save space, but may keep additional metadata or a higher-precision copy to preserve search accuracy — which can partly offset the savings depending on configuration.
  • Replication. A managed provider commonly keeps more than one copy of an index for availability. Two full replicas is roughly double the storage of one, independent of anything about the index structure itself.

None of these are fixed percentages — they depend on the specific engine, its index type, your chosen build parameters (graph connectivity, quantization mode, replica count), and your dimensionality. That is why the Vector Database Cost Calculator asks for an overhead multiplier you set, rather than asserting a single number that would be wrong for most configurations and stale the moment any vendor changed its defaults.

How to pick a multiplier instead of guessing

The reliable way is to measure it, not look it up: deploy a small or representative subset of your data on your chosen provider, read the storage figure the provider reports for that index, and divide it by the raw byte size for that same subset (vector count × dimension × 4, plus metadata). That ratio is your multiplier for that specific provider, index type, and configuration — more reliable than a number taken from documentation written for a different tuning, or from a different engine entirely. Start at 1.0 (no overhead modeled, raw vectors only) if you have no measurement yet, and revise it once you do.

This page states general, widely documented facts about how vector search indexes work. It is not a claim about any specific vendor's current implementation, defaults, or pricing.

Common questions

What is vector index overhead?

The difference between the raw size of your embeddings (vectorCount times dimension times 4 bytes for float32, plus any per-vector metadata) and what a deployed, queryable index actually occupies on disk or in memory. The gap exists because a vector database does not just store your vectors -- it builds a data structure on top of them so that a similarity search does not have to compare against every vector one by one.

What typically causes vector index overhead?

Three common contributors, though the exact mix and magnitude is engine- and configuration-specific: a graph or tree structure (HNSW is the most common) that stores links between nearby vectors so a search can skip most of the dataset; bookkeeping for quantization schemes that compress vectors for search but may keep extra data for accuracy; and replication, where a provider keeps more than one copy of the index for availability, which multiplies storage directly.

How do I pick a multiplier instead of guessing?

The reliable way is to measure it: deploy a small or representative subset of your data on your chosen provider, look at the storage the provider reports for that index, and divide by the raw byte size the calculator computes for that same subset. That ratio is your multiplier for that provider and configuration -- use it, rather than a number from any other source, because overhead depends on your specific index type, dimension, and tuning.
